title: Complete Supabase
summary: Configure the right clients, write CRUD, manage sessions, enforce RLS, and integrate files and realtime events safely.

lessons.title: Clients, variables, and CRUD
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of choosing the Supabase client in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of choosing the Supabase client.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: A Supabase client combines URL, key, and authentication context to issue PostgreSQL and Auth requests. The browser uses anon under RLS, the server may forward a session, and service role stays reserved for tightly controlled privileged work. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: choosing the Supabase client is like a building where Auth issues a badge, RLS checks every door, Storage holds parcels, and Realtime rings on change. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

NEXT_PUBLIC makes URL and anon visible in the bundle, which is intended only because RLS protects data; service role never carries this prefix. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

select lists useful columns, eq translates a filter, order stabilizes display, and range limits volume; data and error form the result to handle. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

Create, read, update, and delete operations pass through policies and domain validation; SDK convenience does not make input trustworthy. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

lessons.title: Auth, identity, and sessions
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of the user session lifecycle in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of the user session lifecycle.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: Auth proves an identity and issues a time-limited session; the application uses that identity to authorize actions, not to trust all client data. Signup, confirmation, renewal, and sign-out are distinct states to render explicitly. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: the user session lifecycle is like a building where Auth issues a badge, RLS checks every door, Storage holds parcels, and Realtime rings on change. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

Email is normalized for usability while Supabase remains responsible for identity; a public message avoids revealing whether a specific account exists. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

When email confirmation is enabled, signUp may return a user without a session; the UI must request confirmation rather than pretending login succeeded. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

A server route rereads the session from a protected cookie and checks expiry; a userId sent in the body never proves caller identity. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.

objectives: Build an accurate mental model of row-by-row authorization.

blocks.text: RLS adds a security filter inside PostgreSQL for every operation and role. USING decides which existing rows are visible or mutable, while WITH CHECK decides which new values may be inserted or retained after update. blocks.text: Storage organizes objects in buckets and paths governed by policies, while Realtime broadcasts already-authorized changes. The server limits size, actual type, extension, and file count; a random name under user.id avoids collisions and path traversal. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

A public bucket fits intentionally public media, while invoices and private documents require a private bucket and short-lived signed URL. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

The Realtime subscription filters user orders but the SELECT policy remains authoritative; removeChannel cleanup prevents duplicate subscriptions and leaks. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.
